name: Protective hairstyle

lead: Protective hairstyles group and secure hair, often tucking the ends away, so there is less combing, styling and exposure to weather and friction. They are used mainly by people with Afro-textured hair, which is prone to dryness and breakage, to keep length and give hair a break from daily manipulation.
Beyond hair care, these styles are a look in themselves and carry long cultural history. Sources describe them as helping retention of length rather than speeding up growth.

paras: Typical styles are braids, twists, cornrows, Bantu knots, locs, buns and wigs. People wear them for weeks, wash with gentle products, moisturize and protect hair at night with satin or silk. Installation by a skilled stylist is common.
Tight or heavy installations or very long wear can strain the scalp and are linked to traction alopecia and tension headaches. Sources advise keeping tension low and caring for the scalp.

angle.text: By reducing manipulation they help people keep length they have grown, and the styles are also a finished look. Sources advise low tension to avoid hairline thinning.

lead: Protective hairstyles are styles that tuck hair away and limit handling and exposure to the elements. They are mainly worn on Afro-textured hair, which tends toward dryness and breakage. Common types include braids, twists, locs, buns and wigs.[1][2]

Wikipedia lists benefits such as shielding hair from temperature and humidity, helping retain length, reducing tangles and giving hair a break from frequent styling and combing.[1] Grokipedia adds that growth rate itself is not changed and that the benefit is retention.[2]

Braids have roots in African cultures going back thousands of years, where styles could signal identity, status or age. Modern use includes self-expression, and in the United States the CROWN Act addresses hairstyle-based discrimination.[1]

paras: The common idea is to keep the hair ends protected and reduce combing and styling. The styles are described as distinct from high-manipulation styles by function.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes braiding in African cultures going back thousands of years, with styles signalling tribal identity, wealth, religion, age, marital status or ethnicity. During slavery many people were forced to shave their heads, and braiding was later restricted by laws not repealed until the Black Power era.[1] Grokipedia dates the origins to as early as 3500 BC.[2]
The CROWN Act of 2022 passed the U.S. House of Representatives and aims to prohibit race-based discrimination based on hairstyle and texture.[1]

Recommended care includes sulfate-free shampoo, deep conditioning, regular moisture and satin or silk wraps at night.[1] Tight styles, especially braids with weaves or wigs, can strain the scalp and thin the hairline, and long wear without care can lead to traction alopecia; heavy styles may cause external-traction headaches.[1][2]
